questions.q: What is a UI Test actually composed of?
options: A sequence of reusable Test Steps that simulate a real user interacting with the actual form, in order
A single Business Rule that runs automatically whenever a form is saved
A screenshot comparison between two versions of the same form
A Flow Designer flow that has nothing to do with Test Steps
questions.explain: A UI Test strings Test Steps together in the same order a real user would perform them.

questions.q: Why does a UI Test need a verification step, not just steps that open and submit a form?
options: Opening and submitting a form only proves it didn't error out — verification confirms a specific, concrete outcome actually happened
Verification steps are optional decoration with no real effect on what the Test catches
A form that submits without erroring always means the logic behind it is correct
Verification steps slow down the Test without adding any value
questions.explain: Without checking a specific outcome (a field's value, a message's text), a Test only confirms the form still loads, not that it behaves correctly.

questions.q: What does the Impersonate User Test Step actually do?
options: Runs the rest of the Test as a specific user holding a specific role, instead of as whichever account launched the Test
Permanently changes the logged-in account for every user in the instance
Deletes the impersonated user's account after the Test finishes
Has no effect on which UI Policies or ACLs apply during the Test
questions.explain: Impersonate User lets a UI Test exercise the same role-based restrictions a real user in that role would actually hit.

questions.q: Why can a UI Test that only ever runs as an administrator miss a real bug in a role-conditioned UI Policy?
options: An admin account often never triggers the condition that hides or restricts a field for a non-admin role, so the broken behavior never fires during the Test
Administrators are blocked from running ATF Tests entirely
UI Policies cannot be configured to depend on a user's role
A UI Test cannot interact with UI Policies under any circumstances
questions.explain: UI Policies conditioned on a non-admin role may be written to exclude admins by design, so an admin-only Test never exercises that path.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does a UI Test confirm that a server-side Test cannot?
options: That the end-user experience through the actual form — including UI Policies and form layout — works as expected
That the underlying server-side logic is syntactically valid JavaScript
That a Script Include's method returns the correct value
Nothing — a UI Test and a server-side Test confirm exactly the same thing
questions.explain: A UI Test is the only ATF step type that exercises the actual form experience, catching UI-layer problems a server-side Test skips entirely.
